inputs.abstract:
This submission fully formalizes and proves in Lean Theorem 6.1 of Denis
Kuperberg's *Positive First-order
Logic on Words and Graphs* (LMCS, 2023): no algorithm decides whether the
language of a finite automaton over a powerset alphabet is definable in
positive first-order logic.

The supporting results are also fully formalized and proved: the positive
Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé game–formula correspondence, the bounded-game
characterization of positive first-order definability, undecidability of
uniform Turing-machine mortality, and the computable reduction from mortality
to positive first-order definability. The submission contains seven concepts
and five completed proofs, with no remaining statement obligations.

The number of letter predicates is part of the input; the undecidability
result is uniform over finite powerset alphabets.

concepts.title: Finite automaton inputs on powerset alphabets
concepts.description:
An input gives the number p of predicates, a finite transition table, and
accepting state numbers. Its alphabet is the full powerset of {0,…,p−1}.
Letters index columns by their binary masks. The initial state is 0.

A table with s rows uses states 0,…,s. A missing entry returns 0; targets are
reduced modulo s+1. This total convention assigns a finite automaton to every
input, without a separate promise of well-formedness. Every ordinary DFA can
be represented (renumber its initial state to 0 and provide its table).
The computability encoding is the standard encoding of natural numbers and
lists, explicitly transported to this record.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax503819.PositiveLogic
import Mathlib.Computability.DFA
import Mathlib.Computability.Primrec.List
import Mathlib.Algebra.BigOperators.Group.Finset.Basic

/-!
---
title: Finite automaton inputs on powerset alphabets
type: definition
---
An input gives the number p of predicates, a finite transition table, and
accepting state numbers. Its alphabet is the full powerset of {0,…,p−1}.
Letters index columns by their binary masks. The initial state is 0.

A table with s rows uses states 0,…,s. A missing entry returns 0; targets are
reduced modulo s+1. This total convention assigns a finite automaton to every
input, without a separate promise of well-formedness. Every ordinary DFA can
be represented (renumber its initial state to 0 and provide its table).
The computability encoding is the standard encoding of natural numbers and
lists, explicitly transported to this record.
-/

namespace Lax503819.Automata

structure Input where
  predicates : ℕ
  transitions : List (List ℕ)
  accepting : List ℕ

instance : Primcodable Input :=
  Primcodable.ofEquiv (ℕ × List (List ℕ) × List ℕ)
    { toFun := fun d => (d.predicates, d.transitions, d.accepting)
      invFun := fun (p, t, f) => ⟨p, t, f⟩
      left_inv := fun _ => rfl
      right_inv := fun _ => rfl }

abbrev Alphabet (d : Input) := Finset (Fin d.predicates)

/-- Binary column number of a subset of predicates. -/
def letterMask {p : ℕ} (a : Finset (Fin p)) : ℕ :=
  a.sum (fun i => 2 ^ i.val)

def Input.automaton (d : Input) : DFA (Alphabet d) (Fin (d.transitions.length + 1)) where
  step q a := Fin.ofNat (d.transitions.length + 1)
    ((d.transitions.getD q.val []).getD (letterMask a) 0)
  start := 0
  accept := {q | q.val ∈ d.accepting}

def Input.language (d : Input) : Language (Alphabet d) := d.automaton.accepts

def PositiveDefinable (d : Input) : Prop :=
  Lax503819.PositiveLogic.Definable d.language

end Lax503819.Automata

concepts.title: Uniform mortality of deterministic Turing machines
concepts.description:
A deterministic machine has finitely many states and tape symbols, and a
partial transition table. Each transition writes a symbol, changes state,
and moves exactly one cell left or right. There is no distinguished initial
state: mortality concerns every configuration.

We use finite tape segments, halting when a transition is absent or the head
would leave the segment. Mortality means that one bound works for every
segment length, every tape content, every head position and every state.
This is the bounded finite-configuration formulation in Section 6.2. It is
equivalent to uniform mortality on unbounded tapes: every finite run uses a
finite segment, and every segment run embeds in an unbounded tape. The
connection to the infinite-run formulation of Hooper's theorem additionally
uses compactness, and belongs to the proof obligation, not the definition.

States are 0,…,states−1 and symbols 0,…,symbols−1, where the stored counts
are increased by one to keep them nonempty. Table rows are indexed by states,
columns by symbols. Missing entries halt; output numbers are reduced modulo
the respective sizes. `true` means move right. These conventions describe
all deterministic machines and give an effective interpretation of every table.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Computability.Reduce
import Mathlib.Computability.Primrec.List

/-!
---
title: Uniform mortality of deterministic Turing machines
type: theorem
---
A deterministic machine has finitely many states and tape symbols, and a
partial transition table. Each transition writes a symbol, changes state,
and moves exactly one cell left or right. There is no distinguished initial
state: mortality concerns every configuration.

We use finite tape segments, halting when a transition is absent or the head
would leave the segment. Mortality means that one bound works for every
segment length, every tape content, every head position and every state.
This is the bounded finite-configuration formulation in Section 6.2. It is
equivalent to uniform mortality on unbounded tapes: every finite run uses a
finite segment, and every segment run embeds in an unbounded tape. The
connection to the infinite-run formulation of Hooper's theorem additionally
uses compactness, and belongs to the proof obligation, not the definition.

States are 0,…,states−1 and symbols 0,…,symbols−1, where the stored counts
are increased by one to keep them nonempty. Table rows are indexed by states,
columns by symbols. Missing entries halt; output numbers are reduced modulo
the respective sizes. `true` means move right. These conventions describe
all deterministic machines and give an effective interpretation of every table.
-/

namespace Lax503819.Mortality

abbrev Instruction := ℕ × ℕ × Bool

structure Machine where
  statesMinusOne : ℕ
  symbolsMinusOne : ℕ
  table : List (List (Option Instruction))

instance : Primcodable Machine :=
  Primcodable.ofEquiv (ℕ × ℕ × List (List (Option Instruction)))
    { toFun := fun m => (m.statesMinusOne, m.symbolsMinusOne, m.table)
      invFun := fun (q, a, t) => ⟨q, a, t⟩
      left_inv := fun _ => rfl
      right_inv := fun _ => rfl }

structure Configuration where
  state : ℕ
  tape : List ℕ
  head : ℕ

def WellFormed (m : Machine) (c : Configuration) : Prop :=
  c.state < m.statesMinusOne + 1 ∧
  (∀ a ∈ c.tape, a < m.symbolsMinusOne + 1) ∧ c.head < c.tape.length

/-- A step on a finite tape; leaving its boundary halts. -/
def step (m : Machine) (c : Configuration) : Option Configuration := do
  let a ← c.tape[c.head]?
  let (q, b, right) ← (m.table.getD c.state []).getD a none
  if !right && c.head == 0 then none else
    let h := if right then c.head + 1 else c.head - 1
    if h < c.tape.length then
      some ⟨q % (m.statesMinusOne + 1),
        c.tape.set c.head (b % (m.symbolsMinusOne + 1)), h⟩
    else none

/-- After n attempts to take a step, `none` means that the run has halted. -/
def run (m : Machine) : ℕ → Configuration → Option Configuration
  | 0, c => some c
  | n + 1, c => (step m c).bind (run m n)

def Mortal (m : Machine) : Prop :=
  ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ c : Configuration, WellFormed m c → run m n c = none

/-- Hooper's undecidability theorem, in its uniform finite-tape form. -/
axiom mortality_undecidable : ¬ ComputablePred Mortal

end Lax503819.Mortality

concepts.title: Positive Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games
concepts.description:
Duplicator must preserve the order and equality of selected positions in both
directions, and the letter order from the first word to the second. In each
round Spoiler selects a position in either word; Duplicator responds in the
other. `Survives` expresses existence of a winning strategy recursively.
A move in an empty word is unavailable, while inability to respond loses.

The two statements are the word versions of Theorem 3.7 and Corollary 3.8.
The formula characterization includes previously selected positions. The
language characterization requires a finite alphabet and a single uniform
round bound for all pairs of words.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax503819.PositiveLogic

/-!
---
title: Positive Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games
type: theorem
---
Duplicator must preserve the order and equality of selected positions in both
directions, and the letter order from the first word to the second. In each
round Spoiler selects a position in either word; Duplicator responds in the
other. `Survives` expresses existence of a winning strategy recursively.
A move in an empty word is unavailable, while inability to respond loses.

The two statements are the word versions of Theorem 3.7 and Corollary 3.8.
The formula characterization includes previously selected positions. The
language characterization requires a finite alphabet and a single uniform
round bound for all pairs of words.
-/

namespace Lax503819.PositiveGames

open Lax503819.Words Lax503819.PositiveLogic

def Valid {A : Type} [LE A] {u v : List A} {k : ℕ}
    (α : Fin k → Position u) (β : Fin k → Position v) : Prop :=
  (∀ i, u.get (α i) ≤ v.get (β i)) ∧
  (∀ i j, α i ≤ α j ↔ β i ≤ β j)

def Survives {A : Type} [LE A] (u v : List A) :
    ℕ → {k : ℕ} → (Fin k → Position u) → (Fin k → Position v) → Prop
  | 0, _, α, β => Valid α β
  | r + 1, _, α, β => Valid α β ∧
      (∀ x : Position u, ∃ y : Position v,
        Survives u v r (Fin.cons x α) (Fin.cons y β)) ∧
      (∀ y : Position v, ∃ x : Position u,
        Survives u v r (Fin.cons x α) (Fin.cons y β))

def DuplicatorWins {A : Type} [LE A] (r : ℕ) (u v : List A) : Prop :=
  Survives u v r (k := 0) Fin.elim0 Fin.elim0

axiom survives_iff_formulas {A : Type} [PartialOrder A] [Fintype A]
    (u v : List A) (r k : ℕ)
    (α : Fin k → Position u) (β : Fin k → Position v) :
    Survives u v r α β ↔
      ∀ φ : Formula A k, φ.rank ≤ r → φ.Realize u α → φ.Realize v β

axiom definable_iff_bounded_games {A : Type} [PartialOrder A] [Fintype A]
    (L : Language A) :
    Definable L ↔ ∃ r : ℕ, ∀ u v, u ∈ L → v ∉ L → ¬ DuplicatorWins r u v

end Lax503819.PositiveGames

statements.signature:
definable_iff_bounded_games : ∀ {A : Type} [inst : PartialOrder A] [Fintype A] (L : Language A),
  Iff (Lax503819.PositiveLogic.Definable L)
    (Exists fun r =>
      ∀ (u v : List A),
        Language.instMembershipList.mem L u →
          Not (Language.instMembershipList.mem L v) → Not (Lax503819.PositiveGames.DuplicatorWins r u v))

survives_iff_formulas : ∀ {A : Type} [inst : PartialOrder A] [Fintype A] (u v : List A) (r k : Nat) (α : Fin k → Lax503819.Words.Position u)
  (β : Fin k → Lax503819.Words.Position v),
  Iff (Lax503819.PositiveGames.Survives u v r α β)
    (∀ (φ : Lax503819.PositiveLogic.Formula A k), instLENat.le φ.rank r → φ.Realize u α → φ.Realize v β)

concepts.title: Positive first-order logic on finite words
concepts.description:
FO⁺ has upward letter tests, the two order tests ≤ and <, conjunction,
disjunction, and existential and universal quantification over positions.
There is no negation of letter tests. A language is FO⁺-definable when one
sentence defines it on all finite words, including the empty word.

`Formula A n` has n available free variables. A quantifier adds variable 0
and shifts the existing variables. Truth and falsity are included as empty
conjunction and disjunction; they are also expressible by quantified order
tests. On a powerset alphabet the test for S means that every predicate in S
holds at that position, precisely the convention in Section 3.1.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax503819.Words
import Mathlib.Data.Fin.Tuple.Basic

/-!
---
title: Positive first-order logic on finite words
type: definition
---
FO⁺ has upward letter tests, the two order tests ≤ and <, conjunction,
disjunction, and existential and universal quantification over positions.
There is no negation of letter tests. A language is FO⁺-definable when one
sentence defines it on all finite words, including the empty word.

`Formula A n` has n available free variables. A quantifier adds variable 0
and shifts the existing variables. Truth and falsity are included as empty
conjunction and disjunction; they are also expressible by quantified order
tests. On a powerset alphabet the test for S means that every predicate in S
holds at that position, precisely the convention in Section 3.1.
-/

namespace Lax503819.PositiveLogic

open Lax503819.Words

inductive Formula (A : Type) : ℕ → Type where
  | truth {n} : Formula A n
  | falsity {n} : Formula A n
  | letter {n} : A → Fin n → Formula A n
  | le {n} : Fin n → Fin n → Formula A n
  | lt {n} : Fin n → Fin n → Formula A n
  | conj {n} : Formula A n → Formula A n → Formula A n
  | disj {n} : Formula A n → Formula A n → Formula A n
  | exists_ {n} : Formula A (n + 1) → Formula A n
  | forall_ {n} : Formula A (n + 1) → Formula A n

def Formula.Realize {A : Type} [LE A] {n : ℕ}
    (φ : Formula A n) (w : List A) (ρ : Fin n → Position w) : Prop :=
  match φ with
  | .truth => True
  | .falsity => False
  | .letter a x => a ≤ w.get (ρ x)
  | .le x y => ρ x ≤ ρ y
  | .lt x y => ρ x < ρ y
  | .conj φ ψ => φ.Realize w ρ ∧ ψ.Realize w ρ
  | .disj φ ψ => φ.Realize w ρ ∨ ψ.Realize w ρ
  | .exists_ φ => ∃ i : Position w, φ.Realize w (Fin.cons i ρ)
  | .forall_ φ => ∀ i : Position w, φ.Realize w (Fin.cons i ρ)

def Formula.rank {A : Type} {n : ℕ} : Formula A n → ℕ
  | .truth | .falsity | .letter _ _ | .le _ _ | .lt _ _ => 0
  | .conj φ ψ | .disj φ ψ => max φ.rank ψ.rank
  | .exists_ φ | .forall_ φ => φ.rank + 1

def sentenceLanguage {A : Type} [LE A] (φ : Formula A 0) : Language A :=
  {w | φ.Realize w Fin.elim0}

def Definable {A : Type} [LE A] (L : Language A) : Prop :=
  ∃ φ : Formula A 0, sentenceLanguage φ = L

end Lax503819.PositiveLogic

concepts.title: Mortality reduces to positive first-order definability
concepts.description:
There is a computable map from deterministic Turing-machine tables to finite
automata on powerset alphabets, such that the output language is FO⁺-definable
if and only if the input machine is mortal. This is the reduction established
in Section 6 of Kuperberg (2023), including the powerset extension in Remark 6.25.

The finite alphabets may depend on the input machine. The quantifier order
requires a single computable transformation, not a separate existence result
for each machine. The configuration alphabet, superposition construction and
integer-game argument will be implemented in the proof package; they are not
assumed in this statement.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax503819.Automata
import Lax503819.Mortality

/-!
---
title: Mortality reduces to positive first-order definability
type: theorem
---
There is a computable map from deterministic Turing-machine tables to finite
automata on powerset alphabets, such that the output language is FO⁺-definable
if and only if the input machine is mortal. This is the reduction established
in Section 6 of Kuperberg (2023), including the powerset extension in Remark 6.25.

The finite alphabets may depend on the input machine. The quantifier order
requires a single computable transformation, not a separate existence result
for each machine. The configuration alphabet, superposition construction and
integer-game argument will be implemented in the proof package; they are not
assumed in this statement.
-/

namespace Lax503819.Reduction

open Lax503819.Automata Lax503819.Mortality

axiom mortality_reduces :
  ∃ f : Machine → Input, Computable f ∧
    ∀ m, Mortal m ↔ PositiveDefinable (f m)

end Lax503819.Reduction

statements.signature:
mortality_reduces : Exists fun f =>
  And (Computable f)
    (∀ (m : Lax503819.Mortality.Machine),
      Iff (Lax503819.Mortality.Mortal m) (Lax503819.Automata.PositiveDefinable (f m)))

concepts.title: Undecidability of positive first-order definability
concepts.description:
There is no algorithm that, given a finite automaton over a finite powerset
alphabet, decides whether its language is definable by a positive first-order
sentence. This is Theorem 6.1 of Kuperberg, *Positive First-order Logic on
Words and Graphs*, LMCS 19(3:7), 2023.

The input includes the number of predicates: the theorem is uniform over
finite powerset alphabets, and does not assert undecidability for one fixed
alphabet. Definability uses the concrete syntax and semantics in PositiveLogic;
algorithmic decidability uses mathlib's partial-recursive computability model.
`ComputablePred` must not be replaced with Lean's `Decidable`, which would
express a different, classically trivial notion here.

import Mathlib.Computability.Reduce

/-!
---
title: Undecidability of positive first-order definability
type: theorem
---
There is no algorithm that, given a finite automaton over a finite powerset
alphabet, decides whether its language is definable by a positive first-order
sentence. This is Theorem 6.1 of Kuperberg, *Positive First-order Logic on
Words and Graphs*, LMCS 19(3:7), 2023.

The input includes the number of predicates: the theorem is uniform over

-/

namespace Lax503819.Undecidability

axiom positive_definability_undecidable :
  ¬ ComputablePred Lax503819.Automata.PositiveDefinable

end Lax503819.Undecidability

concepts.title: Words over an ordered alphabet
concepts.description:
A word is a finite list of letters, including the empty list. Positions are
numbered from zero. The order on words compares words of equal length,
letter by letter. A language is monotone if it is upward closed for this
order; its upward closure consists of words above one of its members.
These are the definitions of Section 2 of Kuperberg (2023).
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Computability.Language
import Mathlib.Data.List.Forall2

/-!
---
title: Words over an ordered alphabet
type: definition
---
A word is a finite list of letters, including the empty list. Positions are
numbered from zero. The order on words compares words of equal length,
letter by letter. A language is monotone if it is upward closed for this
order; its upward closure consists of words above one of its members.
These are the definitions of Section 2 of Kuperberg (2023).
-/

namespace Lax503819.Words

abbrev Position {A : Type} (w : List A) := Fin w.length

def Below {A : Type} [LE A] (u v : List A) : Prop :=
  List.Forall₂ (· ≤ ·) u v

def MonotoneLanguage {A : Type} [LE A] (L : Language A) : Prop :=
  ∀ u v, Below u v → u ∈ L → v ∈ L

def upwardClosure {A : Type} [LE A] (L : Language A) : Language A :=
  {v | ∃ u ∈ L, Below u v}

end Lax503819.Words

proofs.description:
Section 6 and Remark 6.25: the explicit compiler is primitive recursive,
and the positive-game arguments establish its mortality equivalence.

Corollary 3.8, with the finite-rank argument implemented by finite codes of
word positions. The proof uses the proved game theorem through its helpers,
not the concept axiom. Empty languages and universal languages are covered by
empty disjunctions and conjunctions.

The word specialization of Theorem 5.7 (and hence Theorem 3.7).
Soundness is induction on formulas; completeness combines finitely many
separating formulas, one per possible response in the other finite word.

Kuperberg Theorem 6.2: Hooper's arbitrary-configuration construction, the
Post-to-write/move compiler, and finite-window compactness reduce halting at
zero to the approved uniform finite-segment mortality predicate.

Theorem 6.1: a positive-definability decision algorithm would decide mortality
via the proved computable reduction. Both prerequisites are proved in the
proof package; no concept axiom is used in this composition.
